title: Is One List a Rearrangement of the Other?

concept.title: Equal counts, equal contents
body: Two lists are rearrangements of each other when every value occurs **equally often** in both. Count the values of the first list up, then go through the second list and count them down. If no counter ever goes below zero and all counters end at zero, the lists match. Because both lists have the same length, it is enough that no counter drops below zero.
Sorting both lists and comparing them is another way (O(n log n)). The map solution is O(n) and is the model for many "same letters, same counts" questions.

statement: Two lists of `n` integers are given. Print `yes` if the second list can be obtained by reordering the first one (each value occurs the same number of times in both), otherwise print `no`.
inputFormat: The second line has the first list.
The third line has the second list.

examples.note: The first list has two 1s, the second has two 2s.

hints: Count the numbers of the first list in a map.
For each number of the second list, decrease its count.
If a count is already 0 when you need it, the answer is no.

explanation: The first list adds to the counters and the second list takes from them. The lists are rearrangements exactly when no counter is ever missing.
solution.complexity: Time O(n) on average, space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
b = list(map(int, input().split()))

count = {}
for x in a:
    count[x] = count.get(x, 0) + 1
ok = True
for y in b:
    if count.get(y, 0) == 0:
        ok = False
        break
    count[y] -= 1
print("yes" if ok else "no")
